title: An ignition-delay comparison asks one question: does the tuned mechanism sit closer to the measurements than the nominal one, everywhere that matters?
summary: Ignition delay is plotted on a log axis against 1000/T, where a single Arrhenius-controlled process is a straight line. Measured points with error bars are compared with two simulated lines, nominal and optimized. A better mechanism is one whose line passes through more error bars, without moving a good region to fix a bad one.

media.alt: Ignition delay time on a log axis against 1000 over T, for four groups of conditions. Filled squares and diamonds with error bars are measurements; solid and dash-dot lines of matching colour are simulations with the nominal and the optimized mechanism. A legend lists one pair of lines per condition group.

read_the_figure.question: Does the optimized mechanism reproduce the measured ignition delays better than the nominal mechanism, and where does it do worse?
read_the_figure.axes: x: 1000/T in inverse kelvin, so hot conditions are on the left and cold conditions on the right. y: ignition delay time on a logarithmic axis, in milliseconds (figure 08 labels microseconds). Each marker is one measurement with an error bar; each line joins simulated values at the same temperatures.
look_at: Colour and marker shape identify a condition group: an equivalence ratio and a pressure, given in the left legend. The same colour is reused for the nominal (dash-dot) and the optimized (solid) line of that group.
Count how many error bars each line passes through. A line that is close to a point but outside its bar is still a miss, because the bar is the experimental uncertainty.

Look for the bend. On the high-temperature side (left) the lines are close to straight. In the middle of the range the measured delays flatten or even rise as temperature falls, which is the negative temperature coefficient behaviour of large fuels; a mechanism has to reproduce that bend, not only the slope.
Compare the two lines of one colour. Where they overlap, the optimization changed nothing visible; where they separate, check which one is nearer the points.

The other figures in this group repeat the picture for other fuels and subsets: figure 01 compares a literature mechanism with the reduced one (the two lines almost coincide), 06 and 07 show high- and low-temperature targets of methyl butanoate, 11 and 12 test a mechanism tuned on one temperature range against targets in another, using spline-interpolated points.
read_the_figure.proves: That, for these conditions, the tuned parameter set reduces the visible gap to the measurements. It does not prove the mechanism is better outside the plotted conditions, nor that the reduction is larger than the experimental scatter unless the lines move inside the error bars.
if_wrong: Optimized line better in one condition group and worse in another: the objective traded one region against the other; check how the mismatch is weighted across groups.
Both lines far from points in the same way: the structure of the mechanism, not the tuned rate parameters, is the limit.
A line that is smooth where the points bend: the model misses the negative-temperature-coefficient region.
A kinked, piecewise line: the simulated curve has too few temperatures. The kinks in these figures come from joining coarse points with straight segments.
must_check: Log scale on the y axis, and a stated unit that agrees with the other figures in the group.
Error bars visible on every measured point.
Which pairs of lines belong together (the legend must pair nominal and optimized for each group).
A defined mismatch measure if numbers are printed in the legend. Here the symbol epsilon is printed without a definition on the figure.
Whether the points used to tune the mechanism are the same as the points drawn; a fair figure shows held-out points too.
as_drawn: Qualitative reading only, by eye. In the n-heptane figure the nominal and the optimized lines overlap at the hot end and separate in the middle range, where the data bend; the picture alone cannot say whether the movement is toward the data in every group.

terms.meaning: The time from the start of a constant-condition experiment to the sudden temperature and pressure rise. Shorter means more reactive.
A plot of the log of a rate-controlled quantity against 1/T. A single thermally activated step is a straight line whose slope is the activation energy divided by the gas constant.
A temperature range in which ignition gets slower as the mixture gets hotter. It appears as a flattened or rising stretch in the Arrhenius plot of large hydrocarbons and esters.
Actual fuel-to-air ratio divided by the ratio at which the fuel burns completely. Lean is below 1, rich above 1.
Nominal: the rate parameters as published. Optimized: the same reaction list with selected rate parameters adjusted, within their uncertainty, to fit targets.
The experimental uncertainty of one measurement, drawn as a vertical bar. Agreement within it cannot be called an error.
A smaller reaction set derived from a detailed one for cheaper simulation. Two mechanisms that give overlapping lines are, for this observable, equivalent.

remember: On a log axis equal distances are equal ratios, so a visual gap is a factor, not a difference.
Hot is left on a 1000/T axis.
A flat or rising stretch of the measured curve is not noise: it is chemistry (negative temperature coefficient).
Nominal and optimized lines of the same colour belong to the same condition group.
A good fit to the points that were tuned on is expected; the useful evidence is a fit to points that were not.

understand.title: Why 1000/T and a log axis
understand.text: If one step controls ignition, the delay is proportional to an Arrhenius exponential. Taking the log makes that a straight line in 1/T, so curvature in the data is immediately visible as a change of mechanism.

understand.title: Why the curve bends
understand.text: At lower temperature, a different set of reactions (peroxy radical chemistry) takes over from the high-temperature branching. The reactivity of that route falls with rising temperature in a window, and the delay curve bends. Mechanisms that lack that route give straight lines.

understand.title: What an optimization can and cannot move
understand.text: Adjusting rate parameters shifts and tilts parts of the curve. It cannot add a missing reaction pathway, so the shape of the curve is a test of the model, while the vertical offset is what tuning mostly fixes.

steps.title: A single activated step is a straight line
steps.note: Taking the log of an Arrhenius-type delay gives a line in 1/T with slope E_a/R. This is why the figure uses 1000/T on x and a log scale on y.

steps.title: Slope in the units of the figure
steps.note: With E_a in joules per mole and R = 8.314 J/(mol K), the slope per unit of 1000/T is a number of decades. It is steeper for a higher activation energy.

steps.title: Why a ratio, not a difference, is the natural mismatch
steps.note: Delays span decades, so a mismatch in the log is the same size whether the delay is 0.1 ms or 10 ms, and is symmetric: too fast by a factor 2 and too slow by a factor 2 have equal size and opposite sign.

steps.title: Relative error is not symmetric
steps.note: The same factor of two gives +100 percent in one direction and -50 percent in the other. A sum of relative errors therefore punishes slow predictions more than fast ones. Which measure the printed epsilon uses is not stated on the figure.

steps.title: An aggregate mismatch over all points
steps.note: One common way to turn the picture into a number: the mean squared log ratio. It is shown only as an example of the idea; the figure's own epsilon may be defined differently.

steps.title: Why weighting by the error bar matters
steps.note: Dividing by each point's uncertainty means a miss of one bar counts the same everywhere. Without it, precise and imprecise points count equally, and the optimizer will chase noisy points.

worked.title: Slope of an illustrative Arrhenius line
worked.problem: An ignition delay follows an Arrhenius law with an illustrative E_a = 150 kJ/mol. How many decades does the delay change when 1000/T increases by 1 on this figure?

solution.text: Use the slope in figure units.
Insert E_a = 150000 J/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol K).

worked.answer: About 7.8 decades per unit of 1000/T for this illustrative value. The measured curves in the figure are far shallower in the middle range, which is the sign that more than one step is controlling ignition there.

analyze.q: In one condition group the optimized line moves closer to the points at the hot end but further at the cold end. Name two ways the objective could have produced that, and one extra figure that would show which.
analyze.hint: Weights across groups; a single shared parameter that acts differently in each range.

analyze.q: Why can two mechanisms give overlapping lines in figure 01 and still differ greatly in size?
analyze.hint: Ignition delay is one observable among many.

analyze.q: In figures 11 and 12 a mechanism tuned on one temperature range is drawn against targets from another. What does the extra spread of the lines tell you about transfer between ranges?
analyze.hint: What is the model being asked to extrapolate?

evaluate.q: From this figure alone, is the optimized mechanism 'validated'? State the minimum extra evidence needed.
evaluate.hint: Held-out conditions, a defined mismatch measure, uncertainty of the optimized parameters.

evaluate.q: Is a printed single mismatch number per line a fair summary of a curve that fits well at the hot end and badly at the cold end?
evaluate.hint: Think about what an average hides.

create: Redraw the figure with the nominal and optimized lines on separate small multiples, a shared y axis, and a residual strip of ln(sim/exp) beneath each, so the sign of the miss is visible.
Design a leave-one-group-out test: tune on three of the four condition groups, then draw the fourth as a held-out panel.

checks.q: Why is the ignition-delay axis logarithmic and the temperature axis 1000/T?
checks.hint: What does an Arrhenius step become after taking the log?
checks.answer: A thermally activated step gives tau proportional to exp(Ea/RT), so ln tau is linear in 1/T. The log axis turns it into a straight line and the 1000/T scaling gives readable tick values; curvature then signals a change of controlling chemistry.

checks.q: A simulated delay is a factor 2 shorter than the measurement. What is the relative error, and what is the log10 ratio?
checks.answer: Relative error is -50 percent; the log10 ratio is -0.30. A factor 2 too long would be +100 percent and +0.30.

checks.q: The optimized line passes through the points at the hot end and misses the points in the NTC range. What can the tuning not have done?
checks.hint: Which feature depends on the reaction list, not only on rate values?
checks.answer: It cannot have repaired the pathway structure responsible for the NTC bend, or the allowed parameter changes were too small to move that region. The vertical offset is easy to tune; the shape is a structural property.

checks.q: Two mechanisms each have lines that pass through about the same number of error bars. One is half the size. Which is better?
checks.hint: Compare on the purpose of the study.
checks.answer: For this observable they are equivalent, so the smaller one is preferable if cost matters, provided other observables the study cares about are also matched. The figure speaks only to ignition delay.

checks.q: How would you show on a single plot whether tuning helped across all conditions?
checks.hint: Plot the sign and size of the miss.
checks.answer: Plot ln(sim/exp) against 1000/T for nominal and optimized, one marker per measurement, with the error bar mapped into the log ratio, and a band for the experimental uncertainty. Points of the optimized set that fall inside the band and closer to zero than the nominal ones show improvement.
